correctness.rationale: The two-independence face predicate is equivalent to induced maximum degree at most one. Two exact enumeration schemes agree on 62,048 nonempty faces. All 31,003 prescribed codimension-one matching pairs are reconstructed and checked disjoint; a complete topological sort checks all 400,760 directed Hasse covers, visiting every face, so the partial matching is acyclic. Its only critical cells are one vertex and 41 seven-cells. Forman discrete Morse theory then gives precisely a wedge of 41 seven-spheres integrally; no nontrivial attaching maps are possible. An independent complete mod-two boundary-rank calculation corroborates reduced H7 rank 41.

originality.rationale: The cited sources and actual full-text comparisons distinguish this exact Desargues two-independence homotopy statement from earlier ordinary independence, cut, edge-matching, Čech and Rips homotopy statements and from higher-independence classifications under graph-family hypotheses that exclude GP(10,3). Multi-alias published-finding corpus and literature searches did not locate an equivalent or stronger instance. Residual risk from unindexed work remains; search absence is not proof of uniqueness.
residual_risks: Semantic databases do not index every paper, thesis, or unpublished computation; prior unindexed calculations might coincide with this exact invariant.
The original primary papers were materially inspected for their relevant theorems, rather than asserting that every possible article or appendix in the wider literature was exhaustively read.

value.rationale: The Desargues graph is a canonical twenty-vertex cubic incidence graph (GP(10,3), bipartite Kneser H(5,2)), rather than an arbitrarily chosen subgraph. Its two-independence complex has dimension eleven but exactly 41 seven-sphere summands: a full integral homotopy classification beyond the previously known tree, cycle, multipartite and chordal settings. This precise natural invariant provides a reproducible benchmark for nonchordal graph-complex topology. No speculative generalization is needed for its finite mathematical value.
